imo-2013-01.title: Induction on $k$, splitting by parity
imo-2013-01.body:
We use induction on $k$, proving the statement for all $n$ at once. For $k=1$ take $m_1=n$.

Let $k\ge2$ and assume the statement for $k-1$ (and every $n$).

**$n$ even, $n=2t$.** Then
$$1+\frac{2^k-1}{2t}=\frac{2t+2^k-1}{2t+2^k-2}\cdot\frac{2t+2^k-2}{2t}=\left(1+\frac1{2t+2^k-2}\right)\left(1+\frac{2^{k-1}-1}{t}\right).$$

**$n$ odd, $n=2t-1$.** Then
$$1+\frac{2^k-1}{2t-1}=\frac{2t}{2t-1}\cdot\frac{2t+2^k-2}{2t}=\left(1+\frac1{2t-1}\right)\left(1+\frac{2^{k-1}-1}{t}\right).$$

In both cases $t\ge1$, the first factor is $1+\frac1m$ with a positive integer $m$, and by the induction hypothesis the second factor is a product of $k-1$ factors of the form $1+\frac1{m_i}$. This gives $k$ factors in total. ∎

imo-2013-02.title: Alternating polygon for the bound, pairs and strips for the construction
imo-2013-02.body:
**$k\ge2013$ is needed.** Place $2013$ red and $2013$ blue points alternately at the vertices of a regular $4026$-gon, and the last blue point anywhere so that no three points are collinear. Each of the $4026$ sides of the polygon joins a red and a blue point, so each side must be crossed by some line (otherwise its two endpoints would lie in one region). A line not through a vertex meets the boundary of a convex polygon in at most two points, so it crosses at most two sides. Hence at least $4026/2=2013$ lines are needed.

**A useful tool.** If $P,Q$ are two points of the configuration, then two lines parallel to $PQ$, one on each side of it and very close to it, separate $P$ and $Q$ from all other points: because no other point lies on line $PQ$, a sufficiently thin strip around line $PQ$ contains only $P$ and $Q$. (Choose the distances so small that the lines pass through no point.) Every other point is then on the far side of one of these two lines from both $P$ and $Q$.

**$2013$ lines always suffice.** Look at the convex hull of the configuration.
- *Some hull vertex $R$ is red.* A line close to $R$ cuts $R$ off from all other points. Split the other $2012$ red points into $1006$ pairs and enclose each pair in a thin strip by two lines as above. Total: $1+2\cdot1006=2013$ lines. Every red point is now separated from every blue point (by its strip, or, for $R$, by the first line).
- *All hull vertices are blue.* Take two adjacent hull vertices $P,Q$; a line close to segment $PQ$ (parallel to it, on the inner side) cuts $P$ and $Q$ off from all other points. Split the remaining $2012$ blue points into $1006$ pairs and enclose each pair in a strip. Total again $2013$ lines, and every blue point is separated from every red point.

In both cases no region contains points of both colours.

**Answer: $k=2013$.** ∎

imo-2013-03.title: Arc midpoints are equidistant from two of the points (official solution, reworded)
imo-2013-03.body:
Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$, $\Gamma$ the circumcircle of $A_1B_1C_1$, and $Q$ the centre of $\Gamma$, which lies on $\Omega$ by hypothesis. Let $A_0$ be the midpoint of the arc $CB$ of $\Omega$ containing $A$, and define $B_0$, $C_0$ similarly. With $s$ the semiperimeter, the standard tangent lengths give
$$BC_1=CB_1=s-a,\quad CA_1=AC_1=s-b,\quad AB_1=BA_1=s-c .$$

**Lemma.** $A_0B_1=A_0C_1$; the points $A,A_0,B_1,C_1$ are concyclic; and $A$ and $A_0$ lie on the same side of line $B_1C_1$. (Similarly for $B$ and $C$.)

*Proof.* If $A=A_0$ the triangle is isosceles with $AB=AC$, so $AB_1=AC_1$ and everything is clear. Otherwise $A_0B=A_0C$ (arc midpoint), $BC_1=CB_1$, and $\angle C_1BA_0=\angle ABA_0=\angle ACA_0=\angle B_1CA_0$ (inscribed angles on the arc $AA_0$). So triangles $A_0BC_1$ and $A_0CB_1$ are congruent (SAS). Hence $A_0C_1=A_0B_1$, and the angles of these triangles at $C_1$ and $B_1$ are equal, so their supplements $\angle A_0C_1A$ and $\angle A_0B_1A$ are equal too. Therefore $A,A_0,B_1,C_1$ lie on a circle, with $AA_0$ and $B_1C_1$ as opposite sides of the cyclic quadrilateral; in particular $A$ and $A_0$ are on the same side of $B_1C_1$. $\square$

**Which arc midpoint is $Q$.** The points $A_1,B_1,C_1$ lie in the interiors of the sides, so triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ lies inside triangle $ABC$, while $Q\in\Omega$ lies outside it. A triangle whose circumcentre lies outside it is obtuse; say the angle at $B_1$ is obtuse. Then $Q$ and $B_1$ lie on opposite sides of $A_1C_1$; and $B$ and $B_1$ also lie on opposite sides of $A_1C_1$ (the segment $A_1C_1$ cuts off the corner $B$). So $Q$ and $B$ lie on the same side of $A_1C_1$.

The perpendicular bisector of $A_1C_1$ passes through the midpoint of $A_1C_1$, which is inside $\Omega$, so it meets $\Omega$ in two points lying on opposite sides of line $A_1C_1$. Both $Q$ and $B_0$ lie on this bisector and on $\Omega$ (the Lemma for $B$ gives $B_0A_1=B_0C_1$), and both lie on the same side of $A_1C_1$ as $B$ (for $B_0$ by the Lemma). Hence $Q=B_0$.

**Angle computation.** Since $QB_1=QC_1$ and $A_0B_1=A_0C_1$ (Lemma), the line $QA_0=B_0A_0$ is the perpendicular bisector of $B_1C_1$, so it bisects $\angle C_1B_0B_1$; similarly $B_0C_0$ bisects $\angle B_1B_0A_1$. Therefore
$$\angle C_1B_0A_1=\angle C_1B_0B_1+\angle B_1B_0A_1=2\angle A_0B_0B_1+2\angle B_1B_0C_0=2\angle A_0B_0C_0 .$$
The triangle $A_0B_0C_0$ is the reflection through the centre of $\Omega$ of the triangle formed by the midpoints of the arcs $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ not containing the vertices, whose angles are $90^\circ-\frac A2$, $90^\circ-\frac B2$, $90^\circ-\frac C2$. So $\angle A_0B_0C_0=90^\circ-\frac{\angle B}2$ and
$$\angle C_1B_0A_1=180^\circ-\angle ABC .$$
On the other hand, by the Lemma for $B$, the points $B,B_0,A_1,C_1$ are concyclic with $B$ and $B_0$ on the same side of $A_1C_1$, so
$$\angle C_1B_0A_1=\angle C_1BA_1=\angle ABC .$$
Comparing, $\angle ABC=90^\circ$. ∎

imo-2013-04.title: A common point on line $AW$
imo-2013-04.body:
Let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$. Since the triangle is acute, $D,M,N$ lie inside the sides and $H$ lies inside the triangle, on segment $AD$.

**Powers of $A$.** The points $N$ and $D$ lie on the circle with diameter $BH$ (right angles at $N$ and $D$), so $AN\cdot AB=AH\cdot AD$. Similarly $M,D$ lie on the circle with diameter $CH$, so $AM\cdot AC=AH\cdot AD$.

Let $P$ be the second intersection of line $AW$ with $\omega_1$. Since $A$ is outside $\omega_1$ (its power $AN\cdot AB$ is positive), $P$ lies on ray $AW$ and
$$AP\cdot AW=AN\cdot AB=AH\cdot AD. \tag{1}$$
The second intersection $P_2$ of line $AW$ with $\omega_2$ similarly satisfies $AP_2\cdot AW=AM\cdot AC=AH\cdot AD$, so $AP_2=AP$ and $P_2=P$: **$P$ lies on both circles.** Moreover $AP=\frac{AH\cdot AD}{AW}<AW$ (as $AH<AD\le AW$), so $P\ne W$.

**$HP\perp AW$.** If $W=D$, then (1) gives $AP=AH$, so $P=H$. Otherwise (1) reads $\frac{AP}{AD}=\frac{AH}{AW}$, and triangles $APH$ and $ADW$ share the angle at $A$ ($P$ on ray $AW$, $H$ on ray $AD$); so they are similar and $\angle APH=\angle ADW=90^\circ$.

**Conclusion.** Let $\ell$ be the line through $P$ perpendicular to $AW$ (that is, to $PW$).
- $H\in\ell$ by the previous step (trivially if $H=P$).
- $X\in\ell$: as $WX$ is a diameter of $\omega_1$ and $P\in\omega_1$, $P\neq W$, we have $\angle WPX=90^\circ$ (or $X=P$).
- $Y\in\ell$: in the same way, since $P\in\omega_2$ and $WY$ is a diameter of $\omega_2$.

Therefore $X$, $Y$, $H$ are collinear. ∎

imo-2013-05.title: Lower bounds, then squeeze with the fixed points $a^m$
imo-2013-05.body:
**Step 1: $f(nx)\ge nf(x)$ and $f(n)\ge n$** for positive integers $n$ and $x\in\mathbb Q_{>0}$. The first follows from (ii) by induction. By (i) with $(a,1)$: $af(1)=f(a)f(1)\ge f(a)=a$, so $f(1)\ge1$ and $f(n)\ge nf(1)\ge n$.

**Step 2: $f>0$ and $f$ is strictly increasing.** For $x=\frac pq$: by (i), $f(q)f\big(\tfrac pq\big)\ge f(p)\ge p>0$ and $f(q)\ge q>0$, so $f\big(\tfrac pq\big)>0$. Then (ii) gives $f(x+y)\ge f(x)+f(y)>f(x)$.

**Step 3: $f(x)\ge x$ for rational $x>1$.** From (i) and positivity, $f(x)^N\ge f(x^N)$ for all $N\ge1$ (induction: $f(x)^{N}\ge f(x)f(x^{N-1})\ge f(x^N)$). Since $\lfloor x^N\rfloor\ge1$ and $f$ is increasing,
$$f(x)^N\ge f(x^N)\ge f\big(\lfloor x^N\rfloor\big)\ge\lfloor x^N\rfloor>x^N-1 .$$
So $f(x)>(x^N-1)^{1/N}=x\,(1-x^{-N})^{1/N}$ for every $N$; letting $N\to\infty$ gives $f(x)\ge x$.

**Step 4: $f(a^m)=a^m$.** By (i), $f(a^m)\le f(a)^m=a^m$; by Step 3, $f(a^m)\ge a^m$.

**Step 5: $f(x)=x$ for $x>1$.** Choose $m$ with $a^m>x+1$, so $a^m-x>1$. By (ii) and Step 3,
$$a^m=f(a^m)\ge f(a^m-x)+f(x)\ge(a^m-x)+x=a^m ,$$
so equality holds throughout and $f(x)=x$.

**Step 6: all $x$.** Given $x\in\mathbb Q_{>0}$, choose an integer $n\ge2$ with $nx>1$. Then $f(n)=n$ and $f(nx)=nx$ by Step 5, and
$$nf(x)\le f(nx)\le f(n)f(x)=nf(x)$$
(Step 1 and (i)). Hence $nf(x)=f(nx)=nx$, i.e. $f(x)=x$. ∎

imo-2013-06.title: Aligned chords and induction on $n$ (official solution 1, reworded)
imo-2013-06.body:
Call a beautiful labelling of the numbers $0,1,\dots,n$ (on $n+1$ equally spaced points) a *ring of $[0,n]$*; we prove the statement for all $n\ge2$. A *$k$-chord* is a chord joining two labels with sum $k$; we allow degenerate chords (a single point labelled $k/2$). Distinct $k$-chords have no common endpoint. Beauty says exactly: **for every $k$, no two $k$-chords cross.**

Say that one chord *separates* two others if they lie on different sides of it, and call a family of pairwise non-crossing chords *aligned* if among any three of them one separates the other two. Equivalently, the chords can be listed $c_1,c_2,\dots,c_r$ so that each $c_j$ separates the earlier ones from the later ones; then only $c_1$ and $c_r$ can be degenerate.

**Fact (parallel families).** If an aligned family of pairwise disjoint chords covers *all* marked points, then there is a reflection of the circle mapping each chord onto itself. Indeed, with the listing above, there is no marked point between consecutive chords or beyond $c_1$ or $c_r$, so going around the circle the endpoints appear as $p_1,p_2,\dots,p_r,q_r,\dots,q_1$ (where $c_j=p_jq_j$, possibly $p_1=q_1$ or $p_r=q_r$); since the points are equally spaced, the reflection of the regular polygon swapping $p_j\leftrightarrow q_j$ does the job.

Removing a label from a ring keeps it a ring; removing $0$ and lowering all labels by $1$ also gives a ring (the condition $a+d=b+c$ is preserved). The relabelling $x\mapsto n-x$ maps rings to rings and $k$-chords to $(2n-k)$-chords.

## Claim. In a ring, the $k$-chords are aligned, for every $k$.

Induction on $n$; for $n\le3$ there are at most two $k$-chords. Let $n\ge4$ and suppose three $k$-chords $A,B,C$ of a ring $S$ of $[0,n]$ are not aligned. If $n$ is not an endpoint of them, deleting $n$ gives a ring of $[0,n-1]$ with the same three non-aligned chords, contradicting the induction hypothesis; similarly if $0$ is not an endpoint (delete $0$ and shift). So $0$ and $n$ are endpoints; their partners $x,y$ satisfy $n\ge0+x=k=n+y\ge n$, so $k=n$ and $\{0,n\}$ is one of the chords, say $C$. As the three are not aligned, $A$ and $B$ lie on the same side of $C$.

Let $u$ and $v$ be the points next to $0$ and to $n$ on that side, and let $D=\{u,v\}$, $t=u+v$. There are no points strictly between $C$ and $D$; so $D\ne A,B$ (otherwise, say $D=A$, then $B$ would lie beyond $A$ and $A$ would separate $B$ from $C$), and $A,B$ lie beyond $D$.
- If $t=n$: $A,B,D$ are $n$-chords not involving $0,n$ and not aligned ($D$ plays the role of $C$). Deleting $0$ and $n$ and shifting gives a ring of $[0,n-2]$ with three non-aligned $(n-2)$-chords: contradiction.
- If $t<n$: the $t$-chord $\{0,t\}$ does not cross $D$ (beauty; the labels $0<u,v<t$ are distinct), so $t$ is on the same side of $D$ as $0$; since $t\ne n$ and there is nothing between $C$ and $D$, $t$ lies on the other side of $C$. The $n$-chord $E=\{t,n-t\}$ does not cross $C$, so $E$ lies entirely on that other side. Then $A,B,E$ are $n$-chords not involving $0,n$, and they are not aligned: $E$ lies beyond $C$, so it does not separate $A$ from $B$; $A$ does not separate $B$ from $C$, hence not from $E$ either (as $E$ lies beyond $C$); likewise $B$ does not separate $A$ from $E$. Deleting $0,n$ again contradicts the induction hypothesis.
- If $t>n$: apply $x\mapsto n-x$; this keeps $C$, and turns $u,v$ into $n-u,n-v$ with sum $2n-t<n$, the previous case. $\square$

## The recursion

Let $n\ge3$, let $S$ be a ring of $[0,n]$ and $T=S\setminus\{n\}$, a ring of $[0,n-1]$. The $n$-chords of $T$ are $\{x,n-x\}$, $1\le x\le n-1$; they are aligned (Claim) and cover every point except $0$. Say $T$ is of **type 1** if $0$ lies between two consecutive chords of this chain, and of **type 2** otherwise (then $0$ lies beyond an end chord, i.e. $\{0\}$ together with these chords is still aligned).

**Type 1 rings extend uniquely.** If $0$ lies between consecutive $n$-chords $A,B$ of $T$, the $n$-chord $\{0,n\}$ of $S$ must be aligned with $A,B$ (Claim for $S$), so it separates them and $n$ must lie in the other gap between $A$ and $B$, which contains no point of $T$: one possible position. Conversely, insert $n$ there and check that $S$ is a ring. For $k<n$ the $k$-chords of $S$ are $k$-chords of $T$, which do not cross. For $k=n$, the chord $\{0,n\}$ lies between $A$ and $B$ and crosses no other $n$-chord. Now the $n$-chords of $S$ are aligned and cover all points, so by the Fact there is a reflection $\rho$ of the circle with $\rho(x)=n-x$ for every label $x$. If two $k$-chords with $n<k<2n$ crossed, their images under $\rho$ would be two crossing $(2n-k)$-chords with $2n-k<n$, impossible.

**Type 2 rings extend in exactly two ways.** Let $c$ be the end chord beyond which $0$ lies (it is not degenerate, since $0$ lies between its endpoints on that end arc, which contains no other point). The chord $\{0,n\}$ must not cross $c$ and must be aligned with all $n$-chords, so $n$ must be inserted on the end arc beyond $c$, i.e. directly next to $0$ on one side or the other: two positions. Exactly the same verification as for type 1 shows both give rings.

Let $M_n$ be the number of rings of $[0,n]$ and $L_{n-1}$ the number of type 2 rings of $[0,n-1]$. Then
$$M_n=(M_{n-1}-L_{n-1})+2L_{n-1}=M_{n-1}+L_{n-1}.$$

## Counting type 2 rings: $L_{n-1}=\varphi(n)$

Number the $n$ positions of a ring $T$ of $[0,n-1]$ by $0,1,\dots,n-1$ modulo $n$ clockwise, with label $0$ at position $0$, and let $f(i)$ be the label at position $i$. If $T$ has type 2, the family consisting of the degenerate chord $\{0\}$ and the $n$-chords is aligned and covers all points, so by the Fact the reflection fixing position $0$, $i\mapsto-i$, maps each label $x\neq0$ to $n-x$:
$$f(i)+f(-i)=n\qquad(i\not\equiv0).$$
The $(n-1)$-chords $\{x,n-1-x\}$ are also aligned and cover all points, so some reflection $i\mapsto a-i$ maps each label $x$ to $n-1-x$: $f(i)+f(a-i)=n-1$ for all $i$, where $a$ is the position of $n-1$ ($a\not\equiv0$). Combining, $f(a-i)=f(-i)-1$ for $i\not\equiv0$, i.e. $f(j+a)=f(j)-1$ for $j\not\equiv0$. Starting from $f(a)=n-1$ we get $f(2a)=n-2$, $f(3a)=n-3$, and so on, as long as the multiples of $a$ are $\not\equiv0$. If $k_0a\equiv0$ for some least $k_0\ge1$, then $0=f(0)=f(k_0a)=n-k_0$, so $k_0=n$: thus $\gcd(a,n)=1$ and $f(ja)=n-j$ for all $j$, i.e. $T$ is determined by $a$. So $L_{n-1}\le\varphi(n)$.

Conversely, for each $a$ coprime to $n$ the labelling with $f(ja)=n-j$, i.e. label $x$ at position $-ax$, is a ring of type 2. If $w+y=x+z$ then $(-aw)+(-ay)\equiv(-ax)+(-az)\pmod n$; on a regular $n$-gon two chords whose endpoint positions have the same sum modulo $n$ are perpendicular to the same axis, hence parallel, hence they do not cross. And the $n$-chords $\{x,n-x\}$ sit at positions $\pm ax$, symmetric about the axis through position $0$, so $0$ is at the end of their chain. Different $a$ give different labellings (as $a$ is the position of $n-1$ relative to $0$). Hence $L_{n-1}=\varphi(n)$.

## Conclusion

For $n=2$ all $2$ labellings of three points (up to rotation) are rings, so $M_2=2$. Hence
$$M_n=2+\sum_{j=3}^n\varphi(j)=1+\sum_{j=2}^n\varphi(j).$$
On the other hand, for each $j\ge2$ the pairs $(x,y)$ of positive integers with $x+y=j$ and $\gcd(x,y)=1$ correspond to the $x\in[1,j-1]$ with $\gcd(x,j)=1$; there are $\varphi(j)$ of them. So $N=\sum_{j=2}^n\varphi(j)$ and $M=M_n=N+1$. ∎
